analysis.one_liner: Gives oil and gas producers new tax credits, lighter regulation and liability, and freedom to export crude oil.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after being introduced with 16 bipartisan cosponsors, it was sent to eight House committees and multiple subcommittees and died there when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have handed domestic oil and gas producers a package of tax breaks: a per-barrel credit for production from new and low-output "marginal" wells, expanded percentage depletion (a deduction that lets producers shield income based on the value of what they extract), and faster writeoffs of exploration and drilling costs. It would also have rolled back regulation: lower financial-responsibility requirements for offshore facilities under the Oil Pollution Act, a six-year time limit on the government's ability to collect unpaid oil and gas royalties on federal lands, and authority for the Interior Secretary to reduce royalties. It would have repealed limits on exporting domestically produced crude oil, added new procedural rights and compensation requirements for property owners facing endangered-species or wetlands restrictions, and required detailed risk assessments before major health and safety rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas producers, especially operators of marginal and stripper wells and companies drilling new wells, would gain tax credits and deductions. Companies with federal leases would gain from weaker royalty enforcement and royalty reductions. Offshore operators would gain from lower spill-liability financial responsibility, and producers broadly from the right to export crude oil. Property owners facing wetlands or endangered-species restrictions would gain appeal rights and a compensation mechanism.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas producers and operators

how_it_helps.text: Creates a production tax credit of $3 per barrel of crude oil and 50 cents per 1,000 cubic feet of natural gas from new wells and marginal wells, phasing out only as prices rise, and usable against both the regular and the minimum tax [S2] [S3].

Repeals the net income limitation on percentage depletion for oil and gas, expands eligibility for percentage depletion on marginal production, and raises the depletion rate for marginal wells [S2] [S3].

Allows expensing of geological and geophysical exploration costs, expands the enhanced oil recovery credit to secondary recovery methods, and eases intangible drilling cost treatment under the minimum tax [S2] [S3].

Limits the government to six years to recover unpaid federal oil and gas royalties unless the lessee made a false or fraudulent statement, and lets the Interior Secretary reduce royalties owed on federal leases [S2] [S3].

Sets offshore facility financial responsibility under the Oil Pollution Act at $35 million, with any higher amount (capped at $150 million) requiring a risk-based presidential determination supported by clear and convincing evidence [S2] [S3].
Repeals statutory limits on exporting domestically produced crude oil and bars the President from prohibiting or curtailing such exports except from naval petroleum reserves [S2] [S3].

Creates a 'Private Property Owners Bill of Rights': written consent before agencies enter private property, administrative appeals of wetlands and endangered-species decisions, and compensation when an agency action deprives an owner of 33% or more of a property's value or viable use [S2] [S3].

Requires agencies to prepare detailed risk assessments for major health, safety, and natural resources rules, with peer review, petition-based review of assessments, and cost-benefit decisional criteria [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would bear the cost of the new tax credits and expanded deductions through reduced revenue, and the public would receive less from federal oil and gas leases through the royalty limits and reductions. The public would also bear weaker spill accountability offshore and slower or more constrained health and safety rulemaking. In the near term, allowing crude exports could put upward pressure on domestic crude prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and the public treasury

drawbacks.text: The tax provisions cost revenue: a per-barrel production credit, repeal of the net income limitation on percentage depletion, and expanded credits usable against the minimum tax all reduce federal receipts at a time of low oil prices, when the credit's price triggers would leave it fully available [S2] [S3].

The six-year statute of limitations on royalty recovery, limited only in fraud cases, and the Secretary's discretion to reduce royalties would let companies that underpaid on federal leases escape liability, costing the public the royalties it is owed on its own resources [S2] [S3].

Cutting default offshore financial responsibility to $35 million shifts the risk of catastrophic oil spills from offshore operators toward the public, since compensation beyond the guaranteed amount depends on a higher, harder-to-impose determination [S2] [S3].

The property compensation requirement — paying owners for 33% or more of lost value from endangered-species or wetlands decisions — and mandatory risk assessments would make habitat protection and major health and safety rules substantially more expensive to enforce, a cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge [S2] [S3].
Repealing crude export limits could raise domestic crude prices, the opposite of what consumers would want at the same moment taxpayers were subsidizing production [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a broad package for one industry. Its defenders would argue it preserved oil-patch jobs at low prices and gave landowners real procedural rights against federal agencies; those points have some force for marginal-well operators and small landowners. But the core of the bill — production credits and expanded depletion, easier royalty treatment on federal land, lower spill-liability requirements, and freedom to export — transfers public money and public resources to producers while weakening the environmental and fiscal safeguards that protect everyone else. On balance the costs to taxpayers and the public land, water, and health protections outweigh the targeted benefit of keeping marginal wells alive.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 1995 and sent to eight House committees, which passed pieces of it down to subcommittees; none of them ever reported it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Lucas introduced the bill on February 16, 1995, joined by original cosponsors including several other Oklahomans and one Democrat, Rep. Poshard [S1] [S3] [S5].

It was referred to eight committees — Ways and Means, Transportation and Infrastructure, Resources, Judiciary, Commerce, Science, Government Reform and Oversight, and International Relations — a structure that splits a bill apart and makes a single floor vote very unlikely [S5].

Between late February and late March 1995, the bill was referred to six subcommittees, including subcommittees on Energy and Power, National Economic Growth, and the Constitution, and executive comment was requested from the Interior, Commerce, and Army departments [S5].
No committee reported the bill, no floor vote was ever scheduled, and the record shows no action after March 1995, when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers and the public treasury came out ahead, keeping the tax revenue and federal royalties the bill would have given up, along with the existing offshore spill-liability and royalty-enforcement rules. Marginal-well producers and their allies, who wanted the credits and export rights, came out behind.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes, but the 16 cosponsors split 9 Republicans and 7 Democrats, so early support was genuinely bipartisan.

industries.note: The bill hands producers a new per-barrel production credit, expanded percentage depletion, faster writeoffs, weaker royalty enforcement on federal land, and the right to export crude. These gains are paid for by federal revenue and royalties the public would otherwise collect. Sources: S2, S3.
Lower default financial responsibility ($35 million, hard to raise above $150 million) shifts catastrophic spill risk onto the public. Sources: S2, S3.

Repealing crude export limits would let producers sell crude abroad, ending the refiners' access to a captive domestic supply. Refiners' interest in keeping crude at home ran alongside consumers' interest in it. Sources: S2, S3.

industries.industry: Landowners and developers subject to Endangered Species Act and wetlands rules
industries.note: The bill gives these owners written-consent, administrative appeal, and compensation rights when agency actions cut a property's value by a third or more. The cost is borne by agencies' enforcement budgets and, ultimately, wildlife and wetlands protection.
